title: Approximating Maximum Independent Set for Rectangles in the Plane
authors: Joseph S. B. Mitchell (Stony Brook University, USA)
abstract:
We give a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithm for maximum independent set for (axis-aligned) rectangles in the plane. Using a polynomial-time algorithm, the best approximation factor previously known is
O(log log n). The results are based on a new form of recursive partitioning in the plane, in which faces that are constant-complexity and orthogonally convex are recursively partitioned into a constant number of such faces.

a polynomial-time algorithm. The algorithm is based on

Abstract—We give a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithm for maximum independent set for (axisaligned) rectangles in the plane. Using a polynomial-time
algorithm, the best approximation factor previously known is
O(log log n). The results are based on a new form of recursive
partitioning in the plane, in which faces that are constantcomplexity and orthogonally convex are recursively partitioned
into a constant number of such faces.
Keywords-independent set; rectangles; approximation

I. I NTRODUCTION
Given a set R = {R1 , . . . , Rn } of n axis-aligned
rectangles in the plane, the maximum independent set of
rectangles (MISR) problem seeks a maximum-cardinality
subset, R∗ ⊆ R, of rectangles that are independent, meaning
that any two rectangles of R∗ are interior-disjoint.
The MISR is an NP-hard ([14], [19]) special case of the
fundamental Maximum Independent Set (MIS) optimization
problem, in which, for a given input graph, one seeks a
maximum-cardinality subset of its vertices such that no
two vertices are joined by an edge. The MIS is an optimization problem that is very difficult to approximate, in
its general form; the best polynomial-time approximation
algorithm is an O(n/ log2 n)-approximation [9], and there is
no polynomial-time n1−δ -approximation algorithm, for any
fixed δ > 0, unless P=NP [26].
Because the MIS is such a challenging problem in its
general setting, the MIS in special settings, particularly
geometric settings, has been extensively studied. For string
graphs (arcwise-connected sets), an nε -approximation algorithm is known [15]. For outerstring graphs, a polynomialtime exact algorithm is known [20], provided a geometric representation of the graph is given. For geometric
objects that are “fat”(e.g., disks, squares), a PolynomialTime Approximation Scheme (PTAS) is known [13]. Fatness
is critical in many geometric approximation settings. The
MISR is one of the most natural geometric settings for MIS
in which the objects are not assumed to be fat – rectangles
can have arbitrary aspect ratios. The MISR arises naturally
in various applications, including resource allocation, data
mining, and map labeling.
For the MISR, the celebrated results of Adamaszek,
Har-Peled, and Wiese [2], [3], [4], [18] give a
quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme, yielding

In the maximum independent set of rectangles (MISR)
problem on R we seek a subset, R∗ ⊆ R, of maximum
cardinality, k ∗ = |R∗ |, such that the rectangles in R∗ are
independent in that they have pairwise disjoint interiors. Our
main result is a polynomial-time algorithm to compute an
independent subset of R of cardinality Ω(k ∗ ).
Corner-Clipped Rectangles (CCRs). An orthogonal
polygon is a simple polygon1 whose boundary consists
of a finite set of axis-parallel segments. A corner-clipped
rectangle Q is a special orthogonal polygon obtained from a
given rectangle R by subtracting from R a set of up to four
interior-disjoint rectangles, with each rectangle containing
exactly one of the four corners of R in its interior. In
an earlier version of this paper [23], we utilized the full
generality of a CCR, having potentially all four corners
clipped (resulting in a CCR with up to 12 sides). In this
paper we employ a simplified case analysis, and we restrict
ourselves to CCRs with at most one corner clipped, so our
CCRs are “L-shaped” orthogonal polygons with 6 sides, 1
reflex vertex (of internal angle 270 degrees), and 5 convex
vertices (each with internal angle 90 degrees). Refer to
Figure 1. From now on, when we say “CCR” we mean a
rectangle or an L-shaped CCR, with a single clipped corner.

II. P RELIMINARIES
Throughout this paper, when we refer to a rectangle we
mean an axis-aligned, closed rectangle in the plane. We let
[x, x0 ] × [y, y 0 ] denote the rectangle whose projection on the
x-axis (resp., y-axis) is the (closed) interval [x, x0 ] (resp.,
[y, y 0 ]). We often speak of the sides (or edges) of a rectangle;
we consider each rectangle to have four sides (top, bottom,
left, right), each of which is a closed (horizontal or vertical)
line segment. Two nonparallel sides of a rectangle meet at
a common endpoint, one of the corners of the rectangle,
often distinguished as being northeast, northwest, southwest,
or southeast. When we speak of rectangles being disjoint,
we mean that their interiors are disjoint. We say that two
rectangles abut (or are in contact) if their interiors are
disjoint, but there is an edge of one rectangle that has a
nonzero-length overlap with an edge of the other rectangle.
We say that a horizontal/vertical line segment σ penetrates
a rectangle R ∈ R if σ intersects the interior of R. We
say that a horizontal/vertical line segment σ crosses another
horizontal/vertical segment σ 0 if the two segments intersect
in a point that is interior to both segments; similarly, we say
that σ crosses a rectangle R if the intersection σ ∩ R is a
subsegment of σ that is contained in the interior of σ.
The input to our problem is a set R of n arbitrarily
overlapping (axis-aligned) rectangles in the plane. Without
loss of generality, we can assume that the x-coordinates and
y-coordinates that define the rectangles R are distinct and
are integral. Let x1 , x2 , . . . , x2n , with x1 < x2 < · · · < x2n ,
be the sorted x-coordinates of the left/right sides of the n
input rectangles R; similarly, let y1 < y2 < · · · < y2n
be the y-coordinates of the top/bottom sides of the input.
We let BB(R) = [x1 , x2n ] × [y1 , y2n ] denote the axisaligned bounding box (minimal enclosing rectangle) of the
rectangles R. The arrangement of the horizontal/vertical
lines (x = xi , y = yj ) that pass through the sides of the
rectangles R determine a grid G, with faces (rectangular

CCR Partitions. We define a recursive partitioning of a
rectangle B ⊆ BB(R) as follows. At any stage of the
decomposition, we have a partitioning of B into polygonal
faces (CCR faces), each of which is a CCR (meaning a
rectangle or an L-shaped CCR). (Initially, there is a single
rectangular face, B.) A set, χ, of axis-parallel line segments
(called horizontal cut segments and vertical cut segments)
on the grid G that partitions a CCR face f into two or
more CCR faces is said to be a CCR-cut of f . We often
use σ to refer to a vertical cut segment of χ, and we will
consider σ to be a maximal segment that is contained in the
union of grid edges that make up χ. A CCR-cut χ is K-ary
if it partitions f into at most K CCR faces. Necessarily,
a K-ary CCR-cut χ consists of O(K) horizontal/vertical
cut segments, since each of the resulting K subfaces are
(constant-complexity, orthogonal) CCR faces. By recursively
making K-ary CCR-cuts, we obtain a K-ary hierarchical
partitioning of B into CCR faces. We refer to the resulting
(finite) recursive partitioning as a K-ary CCR-partition of
B. Associated with a CCR-partition is a partition tree,
whose nodes correspond to the CCR faces, at each stage
of the recursive partitioning, and whose edges connect a
node for a face f to each of the nodes corresponding to the
subfaces of f into which f is partitioned by a K-ary CCRcut. The root of the tree corresponds to B; at each level
of the tree, a subset of the nodes at that level have their
corresponding CCR faces partitioned by a CCR-cut, into at
most K subfaces that are children of the respective nodes.
The CCR faces that correspond to leaves of the partition tree
are called leaf faces.
We say that a CCR-partition is perfect with respect to a
set of rectangles if none of the rectangles have their interiors
penetrated by the CCR-cuts of the CCR-partition, and each
leaf face of the CCR-partition contains exactly one rectangle.
(This terminology parallels the related notion of a “perfect
BSP”, mentioned below.) We say that a CCR-partition is
nearly perfect with respect to a set of rectangles if for every
CCR-cut in the hierarchical partitioning each of the O(1) cut

The nesting relationship among maximal rectangles.
Consider a maximal rectangle, Ri0 ∈ I 0 . By definition of
maximality, each of the four sides of Ri0 is in contact with
the boundary of BB(R) or with the boundary of another
maximal rectangle, Rj0 . If Ri0 and Rj0 are in contact and
the corresponding edge of Ri0 lies within the interior of the
corresponding edge of Rj0 , then we say that Ri0 is nested
on that side where it contacts Rj0 . For example, if Ri0 is
nested on its top side, where it contacts the bottom side of
Rj0 , then the left side of Rj0 is strictly left of the left side
of Ri0 , and the right side of Rj0 is strictly right of the right
side of Ri0 . For a rectangle Ri0 that is in contact with the
boundary of BB(R), we say that Ri0 is nested on a side
that is contained in the interior of a boundary edge of the
bounding box BB(R). We say that Ri0 is nested vertically
if it is nested on its top side or its bottom side (or both);
similarly, we say that Ri0 is nested horizontally if it is nested
on its left side or its right side (or both). Refer to Figure 3.
A simple observation that comes from the definition, and the
fact that rectangles in I 0 do not overlap, is the following:

are maximal within BB(R), a rectangle Ri0 ∈ I 0 cannot be
nested both vertically and horizontally.

Theorem III.1. For any set I = {R1 , . . . , Rk } of k
interior disjoint (axis-aligned) rectangles in the plane within
a bounding box B, there exists a K-ary CCR-partition of
the bounding box B, with K ≤ 3, recursively cutting B
into rectangles and (L-shaped) corner-clipped rectangles
(CCRs), such that the CCR-partition is nearly perfect with
respect to a subset of I of size Ω(k).

Comparison with BSPs. A binary space partition (BSP) is
a recursive partitioning of a set of objects using hyperplanes
(lines in 2D); a BSP is said to be perfect if none of the objects are cut by the hyperplanes defining the partitioning [7].
An orthogonal BSP uses cuts that are orthogonal to the
coordinate axes. There are sets of axis-aligned rectangular
objects for which there is no perfect orthogonal BSP. A
CCR-partition is a generalization of an orthogonal binary
space partition (BSP), allowing more general shape faces
(and cuts) in the recursive partitioning, and allowing more
than 2 (but still a constant number of) children of internal
nodes in the partition tree.

in the recursive partitioning is h0 + m0 ≥ k/4.
VI. C ONCLUSION
Our main result is a first polynomial-time constant-factor
approximation algorithm for maximum independent set for
axis-aligned rectangles in the plane. Our goal here was to
devise new methods that achieve a first constant factor. Here,
we have given the details for the analysis that gives a factor
4; in the fuller version of the paper [23], we describe a
small refinement that leads to a factor 10/3 and, with further
refinement, to 3 + ε.
In the time since an early draft of this paper first appeared [23], where an initial approximation factor of 10 was
given, Galvez et al [16] have utilized methods built on ours
to obtain improved factors of 6, 4, 3, and now 2 + ε.
More ambitiously, is there a PTAS? Our approach seems
to give up (at least) a factor of 2 (and, with the additional
ideas of [16], only a factor of 2+ε) in its method of handling
the nestedness issue, in order to guarantee enough rectangles
can be charged to nearby rectangle corners. A new idea is
needed for a PTAS, though our methods suggest an approach
to this end, utilizing ever more complex constant-size subproblems generalizing CCRs. Can the running time of an
O(1)-approximation algorithm be improved significantly?
Can the Pach-Tardos Conjecture 1 be resolved?

scheme, we state the following facts (proofs in [23]):

later in the recursive CCR-partition.

it is never the case that both a northwest and a northeast
